rv.q: Despite a surface that might suggest otherwise, it happens too seldom in We’ll See .
Truthfully, she’s all of us — clinging to Nelson’s words for comfort, wrapping ourselves in the warmth of our Apple extended family.
Nelson's group portrait has achieved astonishing depth, and it's a pleasure to spend time with characters who listen to each other so intently and with open minds.
Fun, bubbly and serious all at once, Ms. Blakk is a winner.
With “We’ll See,” Mr. Nelson continues to provide both solace and food for thought.
Watching these plays as both we and the characters age has become a vivid reminder of the passage of time.
Their years of building these people with Nelson have created an intimacy and familiarity that you're not likely to find anywhere else.
Ten years later, all is forgiven, and “We’ll See” felt like a welcome reunion.
It is a rare, or perhaps singular, opportunity for actors, and that alone makes the production a worthwhile experiment in drama.

The cast is composed of some of our finest actors, and together they create something increasingly rare on the stage: a portrait of ordinary people whose simple acts of listening, loving, and showing up for one another become quietly profound.

Thanks to a familiar and remarkable ensemble, and Nelson’s signature fly-on-the-wall naturalism, We’ll See achieves its quiet, bittersweet power by placing larger political concerns alongside the hyper-specific and finely drawn relationships of its characters.
What Nelson’s little bubble of a play proves is that the mere act of coming together, in a theater or over a dining room table, may be the best defense against despair.
And what a joy it is to spend time with the splendid cast of veterans who’ve embodied the Apples on and off for 16 years: Sally Murphy, Maryann Plunkett, Laila Robins, and Jay O. Sanders.
His ability to search for how we can remain human in times of despair is touching.
We’ll See is beautifully acted, carefully observed, and relentlessly uneventful.
Except for that, I had a very enjoyable afternoon revisiting the Apple family.

cn.t: Nelson's Apple family returns after six years to mostly warm reviews, with critics praising the intimate, real-time election night format and veteran cast, though some find the conversational style overly familiar or slow-paced.

vr.q: If this sounds interesting to you at all, I say go check it out.
I found the piece to be a bit long for something without a strong narrative arc, and I personally didn't resonate with these characters all that much.
